evidence: Plaut. Asin. 470: nōn decet superbum esse hominem servom
terms.comment: The usual word, always in a bad sense in classical prose: one who thinks himself above others, and so rude and overbearing (Lewis & Short). The noun is superbia, pride. In poetry it can also be “proud of, splendid” (see proud, pleased).

terms.grammar: adjective, third declension, one ending: the participle of arrogō, “claim for oneself”
terms.comment: One who claims more for himself than is his due.

evidence: Liv. 5.48.9: additus ab īnsolente Gallō ponderī gladius
terms.comment: Its first sense is “unaccustomed, unusual” (verbum īnsolēns, an unusual word, Gell. 1.10.4); from there, behaving beyond what is customary: arrogant, overbearing, especially in success (Lewis & Short).
Also “glorious”; in the sense of boasting as in the title of Plautus’s Mīles glōriōsus.

evidence: Cic. Or. 60: nē quid ineptum aut vultuōsum sit (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: Nimis īrācundē. nōn decet superbum esse hominem servom.
phrases.english: Far too hot-tempered. It doesn’t suit a slave to be proud.

phrases.latin: tumēns inānī grāculus superbiā pennās pāvōnī quae dēciderant sustulit sēque exōrnāvit
phrases.english: a jackdaw, swollen with empty pride, picked up the feathers that had fallen from a peacock and decked himself out

phrases.latin: Contrītiōnem praecēdit superbia, et ante ruīnam exaltātur spīritus.
phrases.english: Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.

sources: Lewis & Short: superbus · Lewis & Short: arrogans · Lewis & Short: insolens
